newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai Jan sugar exports to Japan at 100,000T so far.
newsitem.headline: Thai Jan sugar exports to Japan at 100,000T so far.

text.p: New Thai sugar export declarations for Japan for the first week of January total a large 100,000 tonnes, trade sources said on Monday, although they could not confirm this stemmed from delays in Cuban shipments.
"It's a lot, but not unusual. In January 1996, for example, we exported more than 130,000 tonnes of sugar to Japan," one Thai shipping source said.

"Anyway, I don't hear anything about delays in Cuba. However, we have to see new declarations for the whole month to judge if the amount is unusally big. After all, the figure we see now is only as of the first week of January," he added.

A Thai industry source said earlier that rumours were circulating in the market that Japanese trader Nissho Iwai had bought Thai sugar to replace between 24,000-25,000 tonnes of Cuban-origin sugar previously due to be shipped in January.
A spokesman for Nissho Iwai could not be reached for comment, but on December 11 the company confirmed it was in the freight market for Cuban sugar and quoting January dates.
Hong Kong traders said cargoes of Thai sugar were being shipped to Japan and this was normal practice and was not necessarily to replace Cuban sugar.
"Thailand has already sent about five to six cargoes, maybe more, for January delivery, but I don't think it's to replace Cuban sugar," said one sugar trader at an international firm.
Sugar traders in the British colony said they had not heard of any delays in Cuban sugar shipments.
"Cuban sugar, I don't really know, there may be a bit of delay, but I don't know whether people are using Thai sugar to substitute," another trader said.
Ian Ballantyne, general manager of Australian sugar growers organisation, Canegrowers, said he was sceptical of the rumours.

"Japan does not take much Cuban sugar -- most Cuban sugar goes to China," he said. "It would not be unusual for Thai sugar to be going to Japan this time of year. I wouldn't put too much credence in this story."

On Thursday, China's Economic Information Daily newspaper quoted an official of the cabinet's State Planning Commission as saying the country's ban on imports of sugar for general trade would remain in place in 1997.

China's total sugar supply was estimated at about 7.3 million tonnes a year, with 700,000 tonnes imported from Cuba in 1996 and 1997, the newspaper said. Imports from Cuba are allowed under a special government-to-government trade programme.
